claims.text: An integrated metadynamics approach using machine-learning-optimized interatomic potentials can accurately determine melting properties across a broad range of high-entropy-alloy compositions.
The proposed approach can determine melting properties efficiently.
The target materials are single-phase HEA solid solutions with disordered, multielement configurations.
Equiatomic HEAs may have fcc or bcc crystal structures.
The intervention combines enhanced free-energy sampling by integrated metadynamics with machine-learning-optimized interatomic potentials.
The simulations are to be performed in an isothermal-isobaric ensemble over multiple HEA compositions and crystal structures.
Integrated metadynamics can map complete Gibbs free-energy surfaces containing subtle structural transitions during melting.
Enhanced sampling reduces kinetic barriers associated with observing melting and fusion events.
Resolving melting free-energy differences permits the enthalpic and entropic contributions to fusion to be determined accurately.
The method will predict melting temperature, enthalpy of fusion, entropy of fusion, and volume change on melting within approximately 5–10% of experimental values.
The method will reliably capture key liquid-phase thermodynamic properties.
Traditional simplified models and limited-range simulations are less accurate and lack comprehensive free-energy-surface mapping.
The approach is most applicable when high-quality machine-learning interatomic potentials are available.
Extreme compositions or poorly trained machine-learning potentials may produce deviations larger than the expected 5–10%.
Very high pressures and the extremities of composition space may increase errors because of potential inaccuracies and sampling challenges.
Validation should compare simulated and experimentally measured melting temperature, fusion enthalpy, fusion entropy, and volume change for several HEA compositions.
The approach is falsified if predictions deviate by more than 10% from experimental measurements across multiple compositions.
